1.translation: Śrīdhara says that Hari Himself praises karma-yoga to reveal the meaning of the distinction between “That” and “Thou.” The means of karma-yoga and the means of knowledge-yoga were stated in the preceding two chapters as means to liberation; now He will elaborate karma-yoga through qualities such as offering action to Brahman and through discrimination of the meaning of “thou.” First, praising it as received through an unbroken succession, the Blessed Lord said: “I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvān, the Sun; Vivasvān taught it to Manu, his son; and Manu declared it to Ikṣvāku, his son.” Its fruit is imperishable, and therefore the yoga is called imperishable.

2.translation: Thus the royal sages and other kings who were also sages, beginning with Nimi, learned this yoga as it was taught through the succession beginning with Ikṣvāku and his descendants. Śrīdhara explains the cause of the present age’s ignorance: “O scorcher of foes, that yoga has been lost in this world through the power of time; its succession has been severed.”

3.translation: That same ancient yoga, now that its succession has been broken, has been spoken by Me to you today. Śrīdhara explains that it is being given to Arjuna because he is My devotee and friend; it is not spoken to just anyone, for this is the highest secret.

4.translation: Arjuna, seeing an apparent impossibility in teaching the yoga to Vivasvān, said: “Your birth was later and Vivasvān’s birth was earlier; therefore, how am I to understand that You taught this yoga at the beginning?”

5.translation: The Blessed Lord said: “Many births of Mine have passed, and yours also, O Arjuna. I know all of them because My power of knowledge is never lost; but you do not know them because you are covered by ignorance.”

6.translation: “Although unborn, although of imperishable nature, and although the Lord of beings, I still manifest through My own māyā, having taken My own pure-sattva nature as My basis. I descend by My own will in a pure and exalted sattvic form.” Śrīdhara gives this answer to the question of how the Lord, free from merit and demerit and independent of karma, can take birth like an ordinary living being.

7.translation: Śrīdhara answers the question of when the Lord manifests: “Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and a rise of adharma, at that time I manifest Myself.” Here decline means the loss of dharma, and rise means the predominance of adharma.

8.translation: “For the protection of the virtuous, who follow their own dharma; for the destruction of the harmful, who perform evil actions; and for establishing dharma, I manifest in every age, at each such time.” Establishing dharma means making it firm through protecting the virtuous and destroying the harmful. Śrīdhara says that the Lord’s destruction of the harmful should not be regarded as cruelty, just as a mother is not unmerciful when disciplining a child.

9.translation: “Whoever knows in truth that My birth is self-willed and that My action, in the form of preserving dharma, is divine and beyond the ordinary world, leaves behind bodily identification at death, is not reborn, and reaches Me, O Arjuna.” Śrīdhara adds that the Lord’s manifestation and action are undertaken for the benefit of others.

10.translation: Śrīdhara explains how knowing the Lord’s birth and action leads to attaining Him. Knowing that the Lord, through incarnations of pure sattva, protects dharma and is supremely compassionate, many have become free from attachment, fear, and anger. With their minds absorbed in Him and taking refuge in Him alone, they were purified by knowledge and austerity: Self-knowledge received by His grace, together with the dharma that matures that austerity. Having removed ignorance and its effects, they attained His state, union with Him. This is not a path that began only in the present.

11.translation: If there were partiality in the Lord, He would give His own state only to those who take refuge in Him, not to those who approach with desires. Śrīdhara answers: “In whatever way people worship Me—with desire or without desire—I bless them in that very way, granting the result they seek. Do not think that I neglect those who, leaving Me aside, worship only Indra and the other gods; in every way they follow My path, because I alone am to be worshiped even in the form of Indra and the others.”

12.translation: Those who desire the accomplishment—the fruit—of actions generally worship the gods such as Indra in this human world, rather than worshiping Me directly. The fruit born of action comes quickly, whereas the fruit of knowledge, liberation, is not quickly obtained because knowledge is difficult to attain.

13.translation: Śrīdhara answers the concern that different people act with desire or without desire and that the performers—Brahmins and the other groups—vary in status: “The fourfold order was created by Me according to the division of qualities and actions.” Sattva predominates in Brahmins, whose actions include tranquility and self-restraint; sattva and rajas in Kṣatriyas, whose actions include valor and battle; rajas and tamas in Vaiśyas, whose actions include agriculture and trade; and tamas in Śūdras, whose actions include service to the first three groups. Yet know Me, the creator of this order, to be in truth its non-agent and imperishable, because I am without attachment, effort, or decay.

14.translation: Actions—even actions such as cosmic creation—do not stain Me or make Me attached, because I am free from ego and, being one whose desires are fulfilled, have no longing for the fruit of action. Śrīdhara says that whoever knows Me in this way, as free from attachment to action and its fruit, is likewise not bound by actions, because that knowledge loosens his ego and related limitations.

15.translation: Knowing that action performed without ego and related attachment is not binding, ancient seekers of liberation such as Janaka performed it in earlier ages for the purification of sattva. Śrīdhara therefore brings the teaching back to karma-yoga: “For that reason, you too should first perform action alone—the same action performed long ago by the ancients.”

16.translation: Śrīdhara says this must be examined together with those who know the truth, not learned merely from worldly custom: “What is action, and what is inaction?” Even the thoughtful are confused about what kind of doing and non-doing are meant. Therefore I will explain action and inaction to you; hear it, and knowing and practicing it, you will be freed from the inauspiciousness of saṃsāra.
word_for_word: together with those who know the truth

17.translation: The truth of prescribed action must be understood, the truth of inaction must be understood, and the truth of wrong action—prohibited action—must also be understood. Śrīdhara says that action is not merely whatever bodily activity is commonly recognized, nor is inaction merely the absence of such activity; all three are difficult to discern, for the course of action is profound.
word_for_word: of action, inaction, and wrong action
the course or operation of action

18.translation: Śrīdhara gives two connected readings. First, one who sees inaction in action—action characterized by worship of the Supreme Lord—understands that it does not bind because it gives rise to knowledge; and one who sees action in inaction—the failure to perform prescribed action—understands that it produces demerit and bondage. Such a person, among those who act, is intelligent, a disciplined yogī, and the doer of all action, because all the fruits of action are included in this comprehensive practice. Alternatively, even while engaged in bodily and sensory activity, one may see the Self’s natural freedom from action because the Self is distinct from the body; and one may see bondage-producing action in a merely external renunciation done without knowledge and from aversion to action. The person who acts while established in knowledge of the Self as non-agent is truly joined and established in samādhi.

19.translation: Śrīdhara now clarifies the two meanings established above. Those whose every undertaking is free from desire and the resolve that arises from desire are called learned by the wise. The reason is that, when the mind has been purified through such action, the fire of knowledge born in it burns their actions and reduces them to non-action. In the state of one established in yoga, this also means freedom from desire for a result and from the resolve, “This action must be done for that result.”

20.translation: Moreover, abandoning attachment to action and to its fruit, satisfied by his own constant bliss, and therefore without dependence on anything needed for acquiring or preserving an external support, a person may be fully engaged in natural and prescribed action and yet do nothing at all. His action has become inaction.

21.translation: Free from expectation, with mind and body disciplined, and having abandoned all possessions, he performs only the action required for the body. Even while acting without insistence on being the agent, he does not incur sin or bondage. From the standpoint of one established in yoga, even natural acts such as begging, undertaken only to maintain the body, do not incur the fault caused by failing to perform what is prescribed.

22.translation: Content with whatever gain arrives without being requested, having passed beyond the pairs such as heat and cold and able to endure them, free from enmity, and even-minded in success and failure, he is not bound even while performing the action appropriate to his stage of life—or natural action.

23.translation: For one whose attachment has gone, who is free from desire and from attraction and the other afflictions, and whose mind is established in knowledge, action performed as an offering to the Supreme Lord completely dissolves, together with its latent tendencies; it assumes the nature of inaction. From the standpoint of one established in yoga, “for sacrifice” means that action is performed only to preserve the sacrificial order and for the welfare of the world.

24.translation: Śrīdhara explains that action characterized by worship of the Supreme Lord is itself inaction because it gives rise to knowledge and therefore does not bind; in the state of one established in yoga, even natural action is inaction because knowledge of the Self as non-agent has negated it. The dissolution of action is now elaborated through the vision that Brahman pervades action and all its parts: the offering instrument is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, the fire is Brahman, and the offering performed by the Brahman-agent into Brahman-fire is Brahman. For one whose mind is concentrated in Brahman through this vision, Brahman alone is the destination, not another result.
